task.title: Annotate text with ruby
task.shortdesc: A ruby is a short annotation that stands over or under a word, or beside it in vertical text. In Japanese, it gives the reading of a character, and in other languages it can hold a translation or a note. The vertical text reference lists the properties and the display values used here.

context.p: These terms are used in this topic:

ul.li: The base is the text that is annotated.
The annotation is the short text that goes over, under or beside the base.
A ruby is a base with its annotations.

fig.title: A ruby in horizontal and in vertical text

image.alt: On the left, a horizontal ruby: two bases side by side, two annotations over them, and a wider annotation under both. On the right, a vertical ruby: two bases one under the other, an annotation on the right of each, and a long annotation on the left of both.

context.p: XML has no ruby element, so your stylesheet decides which elements make a ruby. The element names in the examples, such as r, b and t, are placeholders. Use the names that occur in your XML.

step.cmd: Say which elements are the ruby, the bases and the annotations

stepxmp.pre: The word 漢字かんじ has a ruby.

info.p: The annotation is as large as the base unless you set its font-size, so set it, usually to half the size. The font must have the characters, so declare it with @font-face, as explains.

CSSMedia adds the parts that are missing. Text directly inside the ruby element is the base, and annotations without a base are paired with empty bases. White space between the parts is ignored. You write the container elements only when you need them.

step.cmd: Pair the annotations with the bases

info.p: The bases and the annotations are paired in order: the first annotation goes with the first base, the second with the second, and so on. This example has two bases, each with its own annotation:

A single annotation that has no element of its own, directly inside a container of annotations, goes over all the bases of the ruby. When the ruby has fewer annotations than bases, the last bases have an empty annotation. When it has more annotations than bases, the last annotations stand after the last base, on empty bases, and each takes the room that it needs. A ruby that has only annotations, and no base at all, is shown too.

An annotation that has the same text as its base is hidden, and so is one with visibility: collapse. A hidden annotation takes no room, but emphasis marks on its base still stand where the annotation would be, as explains.

step.cmd: Put annotations on more than one level

info.p: A ruby-text-container holds the annotations of one level. A ruby can have several. With the initial ruby-position: alternate, the first level is over the bases and the next one is on the other side of the level before; with alternate under the first level is under. Levels on the same side are stacked outward, each against the one before, with no space between them:

ruby-position chooses the side. over is above the base in horizontal text and on the right in vertical text, and under is the other side. inter-character puts each annotation after its base in horizontal text, as Taiwanese texts do with bopomofo, and acts as over in vertical text. Set the property on the ruby or on its containers of annotations:

Each base and its annotation form a column that is as wide as the wider of the two, and the narrower one is spread over the column. ruby-align says how. space-around, the initial value, spreads the characters of Chinese and Japanese text and leaves half a space at each end. space-between has no space at the ends, center centers the content, and start puts it at the start:
A column is never broken between lines, and the line breaks only where all the levels allow it.

An annotation that is wider than its base can reach over the kana that stand beside the ruby. ruby-overhang: auto, the initial value, allows it, up to half the size of the annotation, and none keeps the annotation inside its column. When an annotation overhangs a character that has an annotation too, the characters keep their place.
With ruby-merge: merge on a container of annotations, all its annotations become one annotation over all the bases. auto merges them only when one of them is wider than its base.

The annotations of a line stand over or under it, and they do not count in the height of the line. When your line-height leaves enough room around the base, the annotations fit in it and the line keeps its height. When it leaves less than the base and the annotations need together, CSSMedia adds the missing room on the side of the annotations, so that the lines do not overlap. If you want equal lines, set a line-height that is large enough, such as 2.
The underline or the overline of a base is between the base and its annotations on that side.

result.p: The words of your document have their annotations, in horizontal and in vertical lines.
